newsitem.title: FRANCE: Parliament backs artists resale right.
newsitem.headline: Parliament backs artists resale right.

text.p: The European Parliament backed in its first reading on Wednesday a plan for European Union legislation to ensure artists throughout the Union receive a slice of the price, whenever their works are resold.
But artists' representatives said it was a mixed blessing.
As things stand some EU member states, notably Britain, do not recognise a "resale right" and so, unlike writers, artists feel none of the benefit when their paintings are resold.

Under the European Commission's proposal artists throughout the Union would be entitled to a harmonised resale right, set on a sliding scale according to the selling price of their painting, sculpture or artefact.

Spanish European People's Party deputy Ana Palacio Vallelersundi, who reported for the parliament, told Reuters she had tried to find a balance between the concerns of major auction houses like Sothebys and Christies and artists.
Sotheby's and Christies say they fear that once the resale right is enforced in Britain it will force the art market to move from London to New York and Switzerland.

But artists organisations say that artists in countries like France and Germany could end up getting less money than they do now because the parliament proposed cutting the percentage artists would receive from a sale.
The parliament voted through an amendment on Wednesday which would introduce a 500-Ecu threshold, lower than the 1,000 Ecus proposed by the rapporteur.
Greens and the European Radical Alliance proposed the lower threshold so that young artists would feel the benefit of the legislation.

The rate of the resale right proposed by the parliament will be four percent of the sale price between the minimum value and 50,000 Ecus, three percent of the sale price between 50,000 and 100,000 Ecus and one percent of the sale price above 100,000 Ecus.
The EU's Single Market Commissioner Mario Monti said the Commission would stick to its more favourable scale of rights.

The authors' organisation GESAC said that under the parliament's proposal a French artist, currently entitled to a three percent resale right, would lose 23 percent on a painting sold for 250,000 Ecus.
In Germany, where there is a five percent resale right, the loss would be 54 percent, it said.
But Palaceo told Reuters that in exchange the French and German artists would for the first time receive money when their paintings were resold on the major London art market.
